title: "Call us to cancel this charge" scams are getting people to dial the attacker
summary: Callback phishing (TOAD) sends a fake renewal or fraud alert with a number to call. Because you place the call, it feels safe, then the 'agent' asks for remote access or a code. Verify charges in your own account; never grant remote access or read a code.

title: Fake "verify you are human" pages are telling people to run commands
summary: A fast-spreading trick ("ClickFix") shows a fake CAPTCHA or error and asks you to press Windows+R and paste a "verification code". The code is malware. Legitimate checks never ask you to run anything.

title: Attackers skip your password with "approve this app" requests
summary: Consent-phishing apps ask you to grant access to your mailbox and files. Because you sign in for real and pass MFA, the only defence is reading the permissions and denying unverified apps.

title: Urgent "confidential" payment requests from the "CEO" are rising
summary: Business email compromise messages push finance and assistants to wire money fast and in secret. The tell is always the same: urgency plus secrecy plus a payment change. Verify on a known number.

title: "Your parcel needs a small fee" texts are everywhere again
summary: Delivery-fee smishing uses a tiny charge ($1-2) to capture card and billing details. If you did not start it, don't tap the link; check the carrier's real app yourself.

title: Repeated login approval prompts? That's an attack, not a glitch
summary: MFA fatigue floods you with approval prompts after your password is stolen, betting you'll tap Approve to stop them. A prompt you didn't start means deny it and change your password.

title: QR codes in emails and letters are hiding phishing links
summary: QR codes in emails hide the real link and push you onto a personal phone outside corporate filtering. Quishing is now the fastest-growing email attack. Don't scan codes from email; re-validate inside the real app.

title: "Your browser is out of date" pop-ups are serving malware
summary: Full-page update warnings push you to download an installer. Browsers update themselves; any site offering a browser update is a trap. Update only from the browser's own settings.

title: Fake IT helpdesks are messaging staff in chat apps
summary: An "external guest" posing as IT warns of a locked account and sends a login link. Verify through the helpdesk you already know; never trust a security link from an unexpected support contact.

title: Suppliers' "we changed our bank details" emails are draining payments
summary: Vendor-invoice fraud is the most common form of business email compromise: a spoofed or hijacked supplier sends a new bank account for the next invoice. Never change payment details on an email; verify on a known number and require a second approver.

title: Fake "please update my direct deposit" emails are redirecting salaries
summary: Payroll diversion impersonates an employee and asks HR to change their direct-deposit account, sending the next paycheck to the attacker. Verify any banking change with the employee through a known channel before actioning it.

title: CAPTCHA-gated phishing pages are hiding behind "you have a voicemail"
summary: Attackers put a fake CAPTCHA in front of credential-harvesting pages so scanners stop probing and victims feel safe, often lured by a voicemail or invoice notification. A CAPTCHA before a login is camouflage, not reassurance.

title: "Enter this code to stay signed in" emails are a new MFA bypass
summary: Device-code phishing hands you a code to type into a real sign-in page; entering it authorises the attacker's device as you, sidestepping MFA. Only use codes you requested yourself, in a login you started.
